This project is an exploration of linear models. Models are estimated by linear regression.  The data set is from Motor Trend magazine.

The assignment is based on estimation of 3 models:
1. mpg as a function of cyl
2. mpg as a function of disp
3  mpg as a function of both cyl and disp

Complete a linear model with data description, a model fit a, and a prediction of mpg based on weigth of 3.050 lbs, with a displacement of 122 cubic inches (this is 2.5 L).

use an anova to compare model 2 with model 3

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
# Load the dataset (built-in)

```{r}
data(mtcars)
```

# View first 6 rows and summary
```{r}
head(mtcars)
```

# Model 1:
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg~wt,data=mtcars, pch=19)
grid()
```

As weight increases, the mpg decreases.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$wt)
```

The value is very close to -1.0, an inverse linear relationship.

### model summary
```{r}
model1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

summary(model1)
```

The vehicle weight has a strong, negative relationship with MPG.

### predicted mpg

# Model 2:

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg~disp,data=mtcars, pch=19)
grid()
```

Similar to the relationship with mpg and wt, the more mpg increases, the more disp decreases.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$disp)
```

This number indicates a strong negative linear relationship.

### model summary


```{r}
model2 <- lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model2)
```

 The vehicles weight is a significant predictor of fuel efficiency, while engine displacement is not very significant at the standard level.

# Model 3 :

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt and disp are the predictors (X's)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
```

 The more the mpg increases, the more the weight decreases, and simular to the weight, the more mpg increases, the more the disp decreases.

### model summary
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
model summary (coefficients, R², etc.), summarize the fit

```{r}
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) and displacement (disp) are the predictors (X's)


# anova: compare models 2 and 3

```{r}
model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

summary(model3)
```

The car's weight is a strong and great negative predictor of its fuel effiiency.

### predicted mpg

```{r}
summary(model3)
```

```{r}
anova_result <- anova(model1, model3)
print(anova_result)
```

# Discussion and Conculsions

According to the data shown, the vehicle weight is a great negative predictor of the MPG, but engine disp is not as significant as vehicle weight when it comes to affecting MPG. The more the MPG increases, the more the weight decreases, and simular to the weight, the more the more the mpg increases, the more the disp decreases.
